title: What steps tell us if three lengths make a triangle?
description: A three-step procedure is written for any three lengths and used on three point five, six and nine, and on four, seven and eleven. Keeko doubts the decimal case and says decimal lengths need a different rule.
teaching_notes: One idea: find the longest length, add the other two, and compare, and the same steps work for any three lengths. Watch for children who think an equal sum is enough, or who treat decimal lengths as a special case.

source: Frame a complete procedure to check whether three lengths can make a triangle, and use it on 3.5, 6 and 9, and on 4, 7 and 11.
video_script.why: The child has seen the three ways two circles can meet on a base and now packs the idea into a procedure that works for any three lengths.
video_script.substitution: The first set is three point five, six and nine, and the second set is four, seven and eleven.
video_script.anchor: Three steps on a card, find the longest, add the other two, compare
video_script.wrong_answer: decimal lengths need a different rule
video_script.wrong_move: A child sees three point five and thinks the steps for whole numbers cannot be used for a decimal length.
video_script.payoff_line: A triangle exists for three point five, six and nine, but none exists for four, seven and eleven.

final_answer.value: A triangle exists for 3.5, 6 and 9; none exists for 4, 7 and 11
final_answer.spoken: a triangle exists for three point five, six and nine, but none exists for four, seven and eleven

never_show: the result for either set before the answer beat
maths_rules: step 2: add the other two lengths
step 3: sum > longest, a triangle exists; sum = longest or sum < longest, no triangle
4, 7, 11: longest 11, 4 + 7 = 11, equal, the circles touch, no triangle
video_script.design: One idea: the three steps work for any three lengths. A card with three steps and two sets; Keeko's doubt closes the video.
